text:
Xi Warned of the ‘Thucydides Trap.’ What Is It?

There is a particular kind of satisfaction in discovering that a problem you assumed was entirely modern was, in fact, named by a grumpy Athenian about 2,400 years ago.

Thucydides was a general who got himself exiled for losing a battle, which gave him considerable time to think about why powerful nations destroy each other. His conclusion was elegant and depressing: it isn’t greed that starts wars between great powers, and it usually isn’t even a particularly good reason. It’s fear. Specifically, the fear an established power feels when it watches a newer, hungrier rival getting uncomfortably good at everything.

Sparta wasn’t afraid of what Athens had done. Sparta was afraid of what Athens was becoming.

Harvard professor Graham Allison picked this up, dusted it off, and gave it a name that guaranteed it would appear in every foreign policy speech for the next decade. The Thucydides Trap. He studied 16 historical cases where a rising power threatened a ruling one. Twelve ended in war.

This is what Xi Jinping reached for when he greeted Trump in Beijing today.

In Xi’s telling, China is Athens. America is Sparta. The message underneath the classical reference is not subtle: We know how this story ends. We would prefer you remembered that too.

Today he sharpened it considerably. If Washington keeps supporting Taiwan, Xi warned, the two countries will face “clashes and even conflicts.”

Beijing always insists the trap can be avoided. What goes unspoken is the condition: only if America accepts China as an equal and backs off.

Thucydides would have recognised the move immediately. He spent years watching powerful men dress strategic ultimatums in the language of wisdom.

He wrote about that too.

text:
The Dog That Might Just Save Your Life

There are approximately 900 million dogs on Earth. This is, depending on your perspective, either a delightful abundance or a logistical nightmare involving an almost incomprehensible volume of kibble. I mention this because science has recently handed dog owners something rather wonderful to feel smug about.

In 2019, a team of researchers at the University of Toronto sat down and did what scientists sometimes do when they want to understand something properly: they gathered up every relevant study they could find, pooled the data from nearly four million people across the United States, Canada, Scandinavia, New Zealand, Australia, and the United Kingdom, and ran the numbers. What they found was remarkable. Dog owners were 24 percent less likely to die from any cause during the study period than people who lived without one.

Twenty-four percent. That is not a rounding error. That is your golden retriever quietly functioning as a cardiologist.

The likely reasons are not entirely mysterious. Dog owners walk more. They interact with strangers more. They experience lower blood pressure, less loneliness, and what researchers politely call “reduced cardiovascular risk factors.”

For people who had already survived a heart attack or stroke, the benefit was even more striking: living with a dog was associated with a 31 percent reduction in the risk of dying. The effect was especially pronounced among people living alone, which, if you think about it for a moment, is the least surprising finding in the history of medicine.

Your dog, of course, has no idea about any of this. He is lying somewhere right now, almost certainly on something he shouldn’t be, dreaming whatever dogs dream about. He does not know he is extending your life. He is simply being a dog: loyal, baffling, and completely devoted to a species that, on reflection, has done rather well to deserve him.
